title: Unit 2: Networks of Exchange

topics.name: Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan routes
The Mongol Empire
frameworkCovers: 2.2 The Mongol Empire and the Making of the Modern World

guide.title: Unit 2: Networks of Exchange: review guide
guide.intro: From about 1200 to 1450, trade routes across Eurasia, the Indian Ocean, and the Sahara grew busier. Merchants carried goods, religions, technologies, crops, and diseases. This unit studies the routes, the Mongol Empire that linked many of them, and the cultural and environmental results.

sections.title: The major trade networks
body: The Silk Roads carried mainly luxury goods (silk, porcelain, spices) overland; caravanserai (roadside inns) and new forms of credit such as bills of exchange made long-distance trade easier. The Indian Ocean network relied on predictable monsoon winds and on technologies such as the lateen sail, the astrolabe, and the magnetic compass, and it could carry bulkier goods by sea.

Trans-Saharan trade grew with camel caravans and improved camel saddles, linking West African gold to Saharan salt and Mediterranean goods. States such as Mali and the Swahili city-states (Kilwa, Mombasa) grew rich by taxing this trade; the Ming admiral Zheng He's voyages (1405–1433) displayed Chinese power across the Indian Ocean.
points: Compare routes by goods, technology, and the states that profited.
Merchant communities settled far from home (diasporas) and spread their cultures.

sections.title: The Mongol Empire
body: Chinggis Khan united the Mongols in 1206, and his successors built the largest land empire in history. After his death it divided into khanates such as the Yuan in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, and the Golden Horde in Russia.

Mongol rulers often relied on local officials and tolerated many religions. By making overland routes safer, they increased trade and the transfer of knowledge, such as Persian astronomy and medicine reaching China, but their networks also helped carry the plague westward.
points: The Mongols destroyed cities such as Baghdad (1258) but also promoted exchange.
Each khanate adapted to local cultures; several later converted to Islam.

sections.title: Cultural and environmental consequences
body: Trade spread religions (Buddhism, Islam), languages, and technologies such as paper and gunpowder. The Swahili language, a Bantu language with many Arabic words, reflects contact between East Africans and Arab merchants. Travelers such as Ibn Battuta and Marco Polo recorded these connections.

Exchange also changed environments. Crops such as Champa rice, sugar, and citrus spread to new regions, and the bubonic plague moved along trade and military routes in the 1300s, killing huge numbers in Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
points: Tie each consequence to the route that carried it.
Environmental consequences include crops, animals, and disease.

example.prompt: Why could Indian Ocean trade carry heavier goods than the Silk Roads?
example.solution: Ships could carry large cargoes cheaply, and monsoon winds made voyages predictable, so bulk goods such as textiles, timber, and grain could travel by sea. Overland caravans were limited to what animals could carry, so they favored light, valuable luxuries.

misconceptions: It was a network of many routes and cities across Eurasia.
They were destructive conquerors, but they also protected trade and moved knowledge across Eurasia.
Trade also spread religions, technologies, crops, and diseases.
They displayed Ming power and brought tribute; China did not establish colonies.

passages.title: Source A: An interpretation of the Silk Roads
text: “The Silk Roads were never a single road but a web of routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, and the Mediterranean. Few merchants traveled the whole distance; goods passed from trader to trader through oasis cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand. Because camels and horses could carry only so much, merchants favored goods that were valuable and light: silk, porcelain, spices, and precious stones. Caravanserai offered travelers food, shelter, and safety, and bills of exchange let merchants avoid carrying large amounts of coin. Ideas and technologies traveled too. Buddhism had followed these routes into China centuries earlier, and papermaking moved from China into the Islamic world and later into Europe.”

passages.title: Source B: An interpretation of the Mongol Empire
text: “In 1206 an assembly of Mongol chiefs proclaimed Temujin as Chinggis Khan. Within decades his armies and those of his successors had conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia, and much of Russia, and in 1258 they destroyed Baghdad. After Chinggis's death the empire split into several khanates, including the Yuan dynasty in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, and the Golden Horde in Russia. Mongol rulers were few in number, so they relied on local officials and generally tolerated the religions of their subjects. Under their protection, merchants, diplomats, and scholars crossed Eurasia more safely than before. Persian astronomers worked in China; Chinese technologies reached the west. So, in the 1300s, did the plague.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the Indian Ocean network
text: “Indian Ocean commerce depended on the monsoons, winds that blow from the southwest in summer and the northeast in winter. Merchants timed their voyages to them, waiting in port for the wind to turn. Ships such as Arab dhows with lateen sails and large Chinese junks carried textiles, spices, timber, and porcelain. Port cities from Kilwa and Mombasa on the East African coast to Calicut in India and Malacca in Southeast Asia grew rich. In the Swahili cities, African and Arab traditions mingled, and many merchants converted to Islam. Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming admiral Zheng He led huge fleets as far as East Africa, displaying Chinese power and collecting tribute.”

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of trans-Saharan trade
text: “Crossing the Sahara became practical only when merchants used camels, which can travel long distances with little water, and improved saddles that let camels carry heavy loads. Caravans carried salt from Saharan mines south and returned with gold from West Africa. The rulers of Mali taxed this trade and grew wealthy. Muslim merchants brought Islam, and many West African rulers converted; Timbuktu became a center of Islamic scholarship with schools and libraries. Trade networks also moved plants. Sugar and citrus fruits spread across the Islamic world, and Champa rice had earlier moved from Vietnam into China, changing what farmers grew and how many people the land could feed.”

questions.prompt: According to Source A, caravanserai mainly served to
choices: produce silk for export
train soldiers to guard the routes
collect taxes on each caravan for the Chinese emperor
give traveling merchants food, shelter, and safety
questions.explanation: The source says caravanserai “offered travelers food, shelter, and safety,” which encouraged trade.
choiceExplanations: Silk was produced in China, not at roadside inns.
They housed travelers, not soldiers in training.
They were inns, not tax offices.

questions.explanation: Pack animals limited what could be carried, so merchants chose goods with high value for their weight.

questions.prompt: Based on your knowledge, how did the Mongol conquests of the 1200s most affect the routes described in Source A?
choices: By banning the export of silk.
By uniting much of Eurasia under one rule, they made overland travel safer.
By closing the routes to all foreign merchants for nearly a century afterward.
By replacing overland trade with sea routes.
questions.explanation: Mongol control from China to Persia protected travelers, a period sometimes called the Pax Mongolica, and trade increased.
choiceExplanations: No such ban existed.
Mongol rulers encouraged foreign merchants.
Overland trade grew under the Mongols.
